utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, if you would like to continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think the translators wanted you to put on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is not on. It is on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 82 in your report, 592, on pages 56 and 57, where you say this: [In English] "Beginning at the latest in September 1991, the SDS followed a two-track approach, publicly. Its leaders advocated ethnic tolerance, democratic dialogue and preservation of Serbian interest within SRBiH and preservation of BH in Yugoslavia through peaceful negotiations with the other national parties, the HDZ and the SDA. Yet secretly its representatives continued to plot, to undermine the joint republic from within -- and made preparations for conflict in collusion with Serbs in Croatia ...," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] I am not reading everything, obviously. This thesis of yours, was it adopted from the pre-trial proceedings or the other way around? The pre-trial proceedings, paragraph 12, where it says: [In English] "Working closely with Milosevic and other Serb leaders, Karadzic pursued a two-pronged approach to ensure that Serbs would remain in a common state, engaging in negotiations to secure a common state, while simultaneously preparing the organs, entities and conditions for the possible ethnic separation and creation of a Serb state carved out from BH, similar to a process that had started in Croatia." [Interpretation] Do you see a striking similarity between your paragraph 82 and the pre-trial proceedings, and can you tell us what was here first? It is an old egg-and-chicken question, so what was the egg and what was the chicken in this case? I would like to correct. It is not pre-trial proceedings, but pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I see your concern. Well, that portion of the pre-trial brief was, in fact, drafted by my team. And as I indicated yesterday, we were engaged in ongoing analysis of all the documentation at our disposal, and I can only suppose at the request of the trial team, they wanted some material on these issues. So we gave it to them for that purpose, and we also used it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in the same report, on pages 57 through 64, under the title "The Serbian Republic of BH and Ethnic Separation," you dealt with this topic. And now I would like to show you what paragraph 12 looks like, in the Defence's submission, and the indictment should look in the following way. Can I please call up 1D03503 in e-court. 1D03503. There is no Serbian version. I'm going to read: [In English] "Tudjman, in respect of Izetbegovic, engaged in negotiations to secure a common state, while simultaneously preparing the organs, entities and conditions for the forcible ethnic separation and creation of a Croat ..." Respectively: "... Muslim state carved out from Yugoslavia, similar to a process that had started in Slovenia." [Interpretation] Here, Dr. Treanor, only the names of the players have been changed, and geographical terms. Is it really that they did what it says here, according to what you knew?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand where this comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is paragraph 12 of the pre-trial brief. However, some changes have been made. It is no longer Karadzic and Milosevic, but Tudjman and Izetbegovic. Did they negotiate in order to preserve Yugoslavia? Actually, they did everything that was in their power to carve out parts of the Yugoslav territory; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. It's not difficult to understand the witness's confusion. The accused can certainly confront the witness with any propositions he wants the witness to address. But done in this guise, extracting portions from one document, then altering it, and not indicating where and how it's altered, and presenting it as an exhibit, is clearly giving rise to confusion. Why don't we just get to the proposition that the accused wants to address and ask the witness to address it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, is that the position, that this is a document that's simply been altered in order to make the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is paragraph 12 of the pre-trial brief. There have been alterations made, and now that the names have been changed, there is more foundation. It is more plausible that Izetbegovic and Tudjman did against Yugoslavia what is ascribed to me in paragraph 12 of the pre-trial brief and paragraph 82 of Dr. Treanor's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, was it your impression that Izetbegovic and Tudjman did what it says here that they did, and did it have anything to do with what we were supposedly doing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only negotiations that I know that Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic were engaged in, regarding the creation of a common state, were in 1994, when the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the confederation between that federation and Croatia were agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that from 1990 to 1992, there were permanent negotiations going on involving the six presidents of the republics and the Presidency of Yugoslavia about the preservation of Yugoslavia, and simultaneously Tudjman and Izetbegovic were setting up their own respective armies and laying down foundations for seceding from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were those ongoing negotiations among the presidents of all the republics in 1991. I'm not familiar with the details of the steps you're -- you have described that they were taking, but I think, in broad terms, that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Professor -- Dr. Treanor. Right here, right here, right here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I am not quite following. What exactly are you agreeing with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statement that simultaneously, Tudjman and Izetbegovic were setting up their own respective armies and laying down foundations for seceding from Yugoslavia, I mean, the trend of Croatian policy at that time was, in fact, toward independence from Yugoslavia, and Croatia was attempting to build up some sort of armed force for itself. And as we've -- I mentioned in my testimony, and in the -- and in my reports, in 1991 the -- there were ongoing attempts by the SDA, that is, the Muslim party in Bosnia, in conjunction with the HDZ, which was the Croatian party in Bosnia, which was, in fact, the Bosnian branch of the ruling party in Croatia, toward independence for BH. And I am -- I understand, although, again, I don't know the details, that certain Muslim groups were attempting to gain arms at that time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D03505 is the next document I would like to call up. Let's just look what paragraph 13 of the pre-trial brief would look in our variant. Everybody can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see that in the original pre-trial brief, it says "Serbs." We are now changing the title of the actors, and we say: [In English] "Earmarked territories considered Croat or Muslim created separate Croat or Muslim institutions to resist Yugoslav authority, declared independence, and forcibly took control of a large part of Yugoslav territory." [Interpretation] Is this correct, what you see on the screen? Did they do that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe you've read that into the record correctly, and it doesn't make any sense to me. Can I just clarify? Which pre-trial brief does this come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to, again, underscore the problems with this kind of approach, and I would like to object to the use of this kind of manipulation of the underlying -- of any underlying documents related to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, if the documents were being, as it were, secretly changed, it would be different, Mr. Tieger. But what Dr. Karadzic is doing is making a point through extrapolating one set of circumstances into another. Dr. Treanor, you understand the point that Dr. Karadzic is trying to make, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, although he made reference in his remarks that are in the record that the Yugoslav authority declared independence forcibly and took control of a large part of Yugoslav territory, which doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, I think we can all see the road down which you're going with this approach, but it might be much more simple to just simply put it directly to Dr. Treanor, rather than do it through this illustrative but somewhat confusing way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, it says in the pre-trial brief that the Serbs did what it says here, that the Serbs did that to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Defence says, no, it was the Muslims and the Croats who did that to Yugoslavia. Do you agree that Muslims and Croats earmarked territories that they wanted to carve out from Yugoslavia, and that they did everything in their power to carry out the unilateral secession?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, as I indicated, Croatia was working toward independence under the new government of the HDZ that came into power in 1990 as a result of elections in Croatia in 1990, and they, in fact, declared independence on June, I believe, the 25th, 1991. They desired to have their independent state consist of the entire territory of the Republic of Croatia, as it had been within the Yugoslav Federation in Bosnia. Certainly, the SDA was in favour of -- was in favour -- certainly after Croatia and Slovenia had seceded from Yugoslavia, was in favour of having an independent Bosnia within the boundaries that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had within the Yugoslav Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're a historian and UN expert. I would like to shed light on the term of the constituency. When it comes to peoples or nationalities, constituency means statehood; in other words, it means that a people constitutes a certain entity? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in Yugoslav legal and constitutional parlance, that is generally correct, although again I'm not a lawyer or a constitutional scholar, but that's my understanding of the use of those terms in Yugoslav legal and constitutional documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D03499 is the next document I would like to call up. 1D03499.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from Oxford Dictionaries. Let's see what the Oxford Dictionary definition is of the term "constituent." It says here, amongst other things: [In English] "Able to make or change a political constitution." [Interpretation] Does this mean that a constituent people implies that such a people has the power to change the political constitution of the state?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me help you. Do you agree that this is an Oxford definition?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? Can the definition be admitted? Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't see any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I object as irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not for me to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Of course, we can admit it, Dr. Karadzic. Dr. Treanor may prefer Yale as opposed to an Oxford definition, but that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1259, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, we will benefit from the fact that you are a historian, and we will show you a number -- a limited number of historical documents and discuss them with you, for the benefit of the Chamber. Those documents are of major significance for the creation and disappearance of Yugoslavia, and the documents originate from a collection compiled by Snjezana Trifunovska. Is it true that you rely on the work of this scientist and that you quoted her in your work?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure -- I think there's a question there, and I'm not sure who you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Snjezana Trifunovska. We can look at your report, 12125, pages 26 and 27, footnotes 109, declaration on Yugoslavia, ICR Press. Let's not call up the document. Everybody can remember. So this is your report, 12125, and you're referring to the name Trifunovska. Let's look at six documents without which nobody would be able to understand the essence of the Yugoslav crisis. Do you agree that on the eve of the First World War, the border between the Austro-Hungarian empire and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia [as interpreted] was on the Drina River? [In English] Kingdom of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the First World War, if I'm not mistaken, the boundary between the Austro-Hungarian Empire and the Kingdom of Serbia was, well, the Danube for quite some distance. The boundary on the side toward Bosnia, I'm under the impression that it was then pretty much as it is today, which would include the Drina for some of its course in the area just south of where it flows into the Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your knowledge is valuable, but I don't have as much time as I requested. So if you could just answer by yes or no whenever possible. Do you agree that Serbs and others lived in the Kingdom of Serbia, whereas west of the Drina, in the Austrian-Hungarian Empire, the residents were Croats, Slovenians, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but especially so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the Austro-Hungarian Empire lost the First World War, and that after the war, it fell into the state of dissolution, it broke up?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that at the moment when the Austro-Hungarian Empire broke up, the Slovenian and Croat peoples, who had lived under the Austro-Hungarian Empire, set up the National Council of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the 29th of October, 1918, in Zagreb, those three peoples set up and proclaimed the state of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, representatives of those peoples did, yes. I believe that's the correct date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the first session of this state, of the state of the Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, decided that the government will be based on the full equality of the Slovenes, Croats and Serbs in that state, and that state was west of the Drina River? We are still not talking about the state of Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in that way, the Slovenes, Croats and the Serbs who resided in the territory of the then Austro-Hungarian Empire, again, after the medieval times, finally won the right to call their state their own? In other words, they became the constituent people of that state?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they certainly claimed that right and became the constituent peoples of that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the 8th November 1918, in Geneva, the Kingdom of Serbia recognised the National Council of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs as the legal government representing those three peoples?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, although I'm not sure about Geneva. I'm willing to accept your word for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that on the 1st of December, 1918, in Belgrade, the National Council of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs asked for and informed King Aleksandar of the desire of this kingdom -- of the state of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs to be independent and to join Serbia, to unite with it in a joint state?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the joint state was proclaimed on the 1st of December. I'm not sure about the sequence of events on that day as you've described them. But, again, I'm willing to accept your word for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we glance at 1D1407. That's the proclamation of the Kingdom of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs. If we can call up this document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it's this Council of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs that asked for and received, at their own request, unification with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we haven't seen the document, but I'm willing to accept what the document says as something that the document says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 85 in this document so that Dr. Treanor can have a look, although he's already familiar with this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The right page, it's underlined: "The Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, who have effected a revolution on the territory of the former Austro-Hungarian Monarchy, have temporarily constituted themselves an independent national state."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further down below: [In English] "In order to realise this idea, the National Council, at its sitting on November 29th, resolved to proclaim the union of the state of the Slovenes, Croats and Serbs with Serbia and Montenegro in one single state, and elected a delegation ...," and so on. [Interpretation] So we can agree that this was, indeed, so; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an expression of the long-standing desire among certain circles among the southern Slavs in the Austro-Hungarian Empire to form a joint state among all the Slavs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 86, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph on page 86: [In English] "With complete confidence, we cherish the hope that Your Royal Highness, together with our whole nation, will strive that, in the end, the frontiers of our state be drawn in such a manner as to agree with our ethnographic boundaries, in accordance with principles of national self-determination as proclaimed by President Wilson of the United States of America and by all the Entente powers." [Interpretation] Would you agree that this new nation, this Yugoslav state, requests and declares the right to preserve ethnic boundaries, invoking the 14 points from the proclamation of President Wilson?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yeah, the document says what you have indicated. I don't think this is the time or place to get into discussions of what exactly the 14 points said about the Austro-Hungarian Empire or what is exactly meant by the Entente powers. Certainly, Italy had certain claims that clashed with those of the south Slavs. But, certainly, in general terms, the new Yugoslav state was looking for ethnic boundaries in the west, certainly, that is, toward Austria, Hungary and Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to look at the right-hand page, the first third or the first half of it, where it says: [In English] "In the name of His Majesty King Peter I, I therefore now proclaim the union of Serbia with the lands of the independent state of the Slovenes, Croats and Serbs in the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes." [Interpretation] Do you agree the Regent Aleksandar says "with the lands of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes"? Serbia is uniting with the lands of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what it says. I would point out that this statement indicates -- is one indication of the different conception that any leaders in the Kingdom of Serbia had about the nature of the state. They saw the state that was being proclaimed as simply an expansion of the Kingdom of Serbia, and conceived that new state to be a centralised state with its capital in Belgrade. And the reference to "lands," I guess, is correct. I don't know what it says in the original, I can't recall. It probably does say the same thing. Of course, I think the "lands" under reference would most properly refer to various provinces which the southern Slavs have been divided among in the Austro-Hungarian Empire; that is, Bosnia, different parts of Croatia, Dalmatia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This says, "the lands making up the state of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs," but, all right, we can agree about that. 1D1407, pages 84 through 86. I'm now tendering it. It's part of the common D number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't remember a reference to 84. But if that was encompassed by the questioning, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these pages will be added to the existing Exhibit D244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more brief point on this subject. On page 88 of the same document, could we look at the Peace Treaty of Saint Germain. Do you agree that this peace treaty from St. Germain on the 10th of September, 1919, the Great Powers recognised the fact that Serb, Croat and Slovene peoples of the former Austro-Hungarian Monarchy united of their own free will with Serbia, in a permanent union, under the title "Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be -- could this page be added to the same document as exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see page 91, Article 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this article stipulates that pending the conclusion of new treaties or conventions, all treaties, conventions, agreements, and obligations between Serbia, on the one hand, and any of the principal allied and associated powers, on the other hand, which were in force on the 1st of August, 1914, or which have since been entered into, shall, ipso facto, be binding upon the Serb-Croat-Slovene state? Article 12 says so?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be added as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm advised that it's already been admitted anyway, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In conclusion, with this picture about the origins of Yugoslavia, could we agree that Yugoslavia came into being by virtue of the fact that the state of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs united with Serbia, and they were joined by Montenegro later, and that's how the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes came into being?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the Serbs never abandoned this constituent status? I'm talking about Serbs west of the Drina. They never gave up on their own constituent status in that joint state?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that they ever did, and I'm not sure how they would have done that if they had wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that that is the basis why, in all the constitutions of the Croatian Republic up to 1990, and in the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was said explicitly that the Serb people, among others, was a constituent people in both these states? That was only changed with the Christmas Constitution of President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know for certain that the reason why the Serbs were mentioned as a constituent people in their Croatian constitutions, which I believe was under discussion here, the postwar Croatian constitutions, goes back to that. I can well see that it might. That gets into the issue of what the nationality policy of the Yugoslav communists under Tito was during World War II. They recognised the rights of other nationalities which had not been recognised in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, so there were more general reasons -- political reasons for them wanting to do that. But it is certainly true that that continued to be the case until the new Croatian Constitution of 1990, which was something that greatly disturbed Serbs not only in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is -- this was a historical aspect, rather than a legal look at all these issues about the creation of Yugoslavia. Speaking of the right of self-determination of peoples in the internal Yugoslav law, do you agree that the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in its introduction, in its preamble, named, as principle 1, the following --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D03506, please. I said "the historical aspect, rather than a legal aspect of these constitutional changes." It's missing from the transcript. Page 3 in English; page 1 in Serbian. Could we zoom in on the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Principle 1: "The peoples of Yugoslavia, proceeding from the right of every people to self-determination, including up to secession, and based on their freely-expressed will in the joint struggle of all nations and nationalities in the National Liberation War and Socialist Revolution, with their historic aspirations, aware of the need to strengthen their brotherhood and unity ...," et cetera, et cetera, " ... united in a federal state of free and equal peoples and nationalities and created a socialist federal union of working people, the SFRY." Do you agree that the Constitution stipulates explicitly that peoples united freely based on their right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says -- it says what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 7 and English page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Article 3 describes the nature of a republic. A socialist republic is a state based on the sovereignty of a people and the government and self-management of the working class and all working people, and the socialist self-management democratic community of the working people and citizens and peoples and nationalities on an equal footing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at Article 5: "The territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia --" In Serbian, we need, perhaps, page 7. No, it's here: "The territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is a single entity consisting of the territories of the socialist republic." And a bit further down, next page in English: "The frontiers of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia may not be altered without the consent of all republics and autonomous provinces." The translation of this document is not good. No, it's fine. Do you agree that for any alteration -- any change in the borders of the SFRY, the agreement of all the socialist republics and autonomous provinces was required?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, yes. But I agree with you, there's a problem at least with what you read: "... the territory, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, is a single entity consisting of the territories of the socialist republics," in the plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And none of these republics or peoples had the right to unilateral secession without the consent of others. That was stipulated in the Constitution, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that some people can infer that from that article. That article, of course, could also refer to the fact that -- or the situation where the federal government may deem it desirable to cede certain territory from one republic to a neighbouring state, for instance, cede some of the territory of the Republic of Serbia to Bulgaria, and this article would give, basically, the Republic of Serbia the right to veto that and that they would have to agree to that themselves. The majority of republics and the government and so forth couldn't force that on them. So there are different situations that this could apply, and the people you're referring to, some people could certainly interpret it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be received?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection to the pages referenced, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Those can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1260, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at what goes on with the Republic of Croatia in this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D03507, page 2, the fundamental principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can all read for ourselves, "Basic Provisions." Is it the case that Article 1 says that the Serb people -- the Croatian people, and the Serbian people, and other peoples established the state of Croatia, the Socialist Republic of Croatia, and on the basis of a right to self-determination, including the right to secede and unite with other nations, through its freely-expressed will, et cetera, et cetera, and based on that freedom to express their will, they all united into the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Do you agree that this basic provision of the Croatian Constitution recognises the right of the Serbs to self-determination because they formed, together with others, the state of Croatia, based on their own free will?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it says -- it says what it says. As in the previous document that we saw, the analogous article in the Constitution of the SFRY, I would just have to comment that I think a few people would contest how freely-expressed the wills of these various people was at that time, but that's certainly what this article says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please go to page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are general provisions, Article 1. In the second paragraph, it says: "The Socialist Republic of Croatia is a national state of the Croatian people, a state of the Serbian people in Croatia, and a state of nationalities residing therein." Do you agree that this reflected on paragraph 27 in your report? I will read it. I don't want to call it up. The second sentence reads: [In English] "The constitution dropped the reference in Croatia's 1974 Constitution to the Serbs as one of the constituent people of the republic, although it did guarantee national equality in Article 3." [Interpretation] This is your document, 65 ter 12125, paragraph 27, page 14. And further on, you say: "The Republic of Croatia stays in Yugoslavia" - you quote from Article 140 - "until a new agreement is reached by the Yugoslav Republics or until the moment the Croatian Parliament issues a decision to do differently." Do you agree that was what the situation was like in Croatia until the moment the Croatian Constitution was changed in 1991, when the crisis broke out? The year is 1990, when the Constitution was changed.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I understand you correctly, the situation is as I described it in the report, in the leadership study.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in 1990, changes were made, contrary to the wishes and desires of one of the two constituent peoples in Croatia at that moment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in general terms, I agree with that. It gets into issues of who the representatives were and that sort of thing. Perhaps it would help the Court for me to comment that the political position of the Serbs and their political parties in Croatia was much different after the 1990 elections than it was in Bosnia. In the elections in Croatia in 1990, multi-party elections, only a very small number of Serbian deputies were elected, and I think only one or two from the SDS, whereas in Bosnia, as we've seen, they had a very, very strong position, having almost a third of the deputies in the Bosnian chambers. So their opportunities to make their desires known were not as good as the Serbs in Bosnia. But in general terms, I would certainly agree with that comment that most Serbs in Croatia were probably dissatisfied with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, and then we will move on to Bosnia, because you're right, we should return to Bosnia from Croatia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those were the two pages referenced, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. The two pages referenced will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1261, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D03508 is the next document I would like to call up. Let's keep page 1 in English, and can we look at page 8 in the Serbian version of the document. Before I put my question to you, I would like to draw your attention to the three provisions of the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Here, we see number 1, where it says that the Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and members of other peoples and nationalities, together with all the other peoples and nationalities of Yugoslavia, established a revolutionary peoples democratic power within the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and that they created the National Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The following page in English. I would like to ask all participants to look at paragraph 1, where it says they created the People's Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then can we look at page 9 in Serbian and page 2 in English. Or, rather, no, we can stay with this page in English. The English page is good. The following page is Serbian. Now, Article 2, where it says: "The workers and citizens, the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats, Serbs and Muslims, as well as the members of other nations and national minorities, will realise in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a state and a community organised on the principles of self-management, their sovereign rights, and the interests of their class and nation," "of their class and nation." And now can we go to page 27 in Serbian and page 15 in English. Article 1 in the first part, the end of the article reads: "The nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, members of other nations and nationalities living in it, is founded on the authority and self-management of the working class, all working people, and the sovereignty and equality of all the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and members of other nations and nationalities living in it." And then in Article 2, I would like to draw your attention to the following: "The working people and citizens, the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbs, Croats and Muslims, and members of other nations and nationalities, shall realise their sovereign rights in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ...," and so on and so forth. Article 3, where it says: "The equality of the nations and nationalities and their members is guaranteed in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that there is no doubt that the three peoples that constitute Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, are, indeed, constituent peoples with absolutely equal rights?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree that these articles say what they say. But getting directly to your question, I would have to say yes. But the interesting point is there's repeated reference to other nations and nationalities having the same rights, and in all the controversies we've been discussing in connection with my reports, the rights of those nations and nationalities don't get a mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Treanor, do you remember the seven members of the Presidency was supposed to represent those other peoples and nationalities in the Presidency; two Croats, two Muslims and two Serbs, and one representing everybody else; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, representing everybody else in that particular institution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can these pages be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Those referenced articles, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1262, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 16278 is the next document I would like to call up. 16278.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You, yourself, stated that the amendments to the Constitution which were adopted on the 31st of July, 1990, somewhat altered the Constitution. Let us now look at Amendment 60, which is on page 1 both in the Serbian and English versions. Amendment 60 also confirms and guarantees the constituent quality of the three peoples. It says here: "The Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a democratic, sovereign state of the equal citizens and peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, and members of other nations and nationalities that live there." And now let's look at Amendment 49. 49, yes, we can see it. Paragraph 2 says: "Political organisation and activity directed at the following shall be forbidden: forcibly changing the constitutionally-established order; threatening the territorial integrity and independence of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia or the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you agree that the constitutions of Yugoslavia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as new constitutional amendments to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, guaranteed the rights of the peoples, including Serbs who were constituent peoples, both in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the articles you've read say what they say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1263, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the provisions of the SFRY, as well as the amendments to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, ban political organisation and activity directed at threatening the territorial integrity and independence of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia? Let me remind you that that amendment was adopted in 1990 on the very eve of the elections. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've just see the amendment to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am familiar with the fact that there were packages of amendments made to the SFRY Constitution as well. If there was an analogous amendment there, I'm willing to take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And can we now look at 65 ter -- first of all, can this be admitted? Has it been admitted? Yes. Okay. 65 ter 16278, pages 2 and 3; 2 and 3 in Serbian, and 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, let me ask you this: Do you remember, since you said in your report that the Serbian Democratic Party, in July 1990, immediately after it was set up and before the constitutional amendments were adopted, demanded for a two-tier parliament to be introduced, or, in other words, that there should be a house of the peoples in the government; however, their efforts were in vain, the proposal was never adopted? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I believe I mentioned that in my testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at bullet point 10, where it says: "A council shall be formed within the SRBH Assembly for the matter of ensuring the equality of the nations and nationalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina." On behalf of our peoples and nationalities, I apologise for this awkward language. Would this have been a replacement for the Council of Peoples or National Council that we requested; in other words, that that body would have had the same authorities that we asked for?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly seems to be conceived in that spirit, but this council does not have the same status as a chamber of the Assembly. A chamber would have been immediately constituted with the other chambers. Unfortunately, this council was never -- was never constituted. That was an action that had to be taken by the Assembly, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was also an answer to the question I don't have to put. Can you look at the following: "The council shall examine matters that relate to the equality of languages and scripts; the organisation and activities of cultural institutions ...," and so on and so forth: "If at least 20 deputies consider that a proposed regulation or other act within the competence of the SRBH Assembly violates the equality of nations and nationalities, the draft to go before the SRBH Assembly for identification shall be defined by the council. "The SRBH Assembly shall render decisions on matters concerning the fulfillment of the equality of the nations and nationalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the proposal of the council, through a special procedure established by the SRBH Assembly Rules of Procedure ...," and so on and so forth. Do you agree, therefore, that when vital interests of a people are at stake, it takes only 20 deputies to raise that issue, and that that issue cannot be resolved before a recommendation is received from the council with regard to that specific issue ?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it seems to say. I think my testimony touched on that a little bit. It is also discussed in the report or mentioned in the report in connection with the attempt in February 1991 to pass a declaration on the sovereignty of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on two occasions, that council helped Avdo Campara explain that decisions could not be reached before an opinion of the council was received, and that the same person, on the 15th of October, 1991, decided that things could be done differently without that decision having been preceded by any new legal instruments?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to Mr. Campara, I believe. Yes, he did say that in February. I believe there's reference in the report. What he exactly said in October at that session, I don't know, but that's certainly what they did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? Can these pages be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it was just page 2 was referenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be the case. So page 2 can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2 and 3 in Serbian and 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: All those referenced, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be added to the existing Exhibit D1263, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the decision on organising a referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina was adopted, according to the procedure prescribed in bullet point 5, line 9, of Amendment 71 to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which envisages that the Assembly of the SRBH can organise a referendum at a joint session of its two councils? I'm afraid I was speeding along, so it hasn't been recorded that the referendum in question is the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we see 65 ter 6228 to make things easier for you. 6228, page -- it's a decision, so there is just one page. No need to reference the page. Can we look at the left-hand-side page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says, in the preamble, that that referendum can be called pursuant to Amendment 71, paragraph 5, line 2, of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina? I just want us to identify the amendment in question, and then we will actually look at the amendment, itself. Do we agree on the number of the amendment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that page can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1264, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 16278 is the next document I would like to call up. 16278, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have just called up Amendment 71, paragraph 5 thereof, paragraph 5, where it says -- let's look at line 9, where it says they call republican referenda. Do you agree that it was up to the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to call the referendum, and that that right arose from the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Article 152? Do you agree or do you want me to call up the Constitution for your perusal, and maybe that will help you to agree if you can't agree with me now? Do you agree that this is Amendment 70 [as interpreted], paragraph 5, where it says that the Assembly has the right to call up the republican referenda?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to say that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the page be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it can, Dr. Karadzic. But I'm thinking that where the question encompasses the point you want to make, and the witness agrees with it, it's already in the transcript, so quite often we're admitting documents which do no more than reflect that which we already have in the transcript. So this can be admitted, but bear that in mind for the future, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it will be added to Exhibit D1263.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll try not to burden the file. However, sometimes it seems to be necessary. Can we now look at 1D3508. Let's see what the nature was of that republican referendum. 1D3508, page 89 in Serbian and 60 in English. 60 in English, Article 152.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "The assembly of the socio-political unit may declare a referendum for the prior declaration of working people on particular issues within the competence of the assembly, or for the confirmation of laws, ordinances, or other general regulations. The decision reached by such a referendum is binding." Do we agree that it says here that this is a prior declaration of opinion, an opinion that precedes the decision that will finally be made by that socio-political unit? Do we agree on that? It hasn't been recorded that this referendum may be declared only in relation to an issue within the competence of that socio-political unit, only within its own competence.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be added to 1262, D1262?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, did you have all those documents? Were they accessible to you when you drafted your reports? Were they provided to you by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were certainly accessible to me, and they were accessible to me because I had collected them myself or directed that they be collected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we'll break there until 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe the last page has not yet been admitted. If we could check. I would like to tender it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, we will admit it, but it actually falls directly into the category of those items which I suggested are just as valuable in the transcript. But we will admit it on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be added to Exhibit D1262, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll deal for a while longer for the basis for the referendum. 1D3519 is the next document I would like to call up. It's the Law on Referendum, page 3, Article 3, to establish what the Law on Referendum stipulates. Article 26, Article 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says that the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina may call a referendum on matters from its own purview, matters in its jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not able to decide about the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia, it was not within its competence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the issue there would be the relationship of the republic to the rest of the federation. I'm not aware of what the Constitution of the SRBH might say on that issue or be construed to say on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I will read the third and fourth paragraph of Article 5 of the Constitution of Yugoslavia, which we've looked at before: "The borders of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia may not be altered without the consent of all the republics and autonomous provinces, whereas the borders between republics may be altered only on the basis of their mutual agreement." So the issue of territorial integrity of Yugoslavia falls under the purview of the Yugoslav Assembly and is stipulated in the Yugoslav Constitution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think we discussed that earlier. I said this could simply refer to the drawing of particular lines. I think the issue of independences or changing the relationship between the republic and the federation is a different one. And as I say, I can't recall at this point. I would have to refresh my memory, looking at the Constitution in its entirety as to what exactly is there on that issue or could be construed to be on that issue, bearing in mind that I'm not a legal expert or a constitutional scholar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good, then we can move on. Can we see 1D3509.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that changing borders that the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina could decide about would be the changing of the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina with other republics, the so-called administrative borders between federal units? Page 2 in Serbian; page 3 in English. Amendment 62, paragraph 1, line 2, says: "The borders of republics -- the borders of the republic may be changed by the Republic of BH, based on the freely-expressed will of the people and a public referendum, with the two-third majority vote of the entire electorate"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. That's what it seems to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So even a minimal change in the administrative borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia required a positive response of two-thirds of the entire electorate. Do you agree that changing the status of a republic, in the context of Yugoslavia, is a much bigger issue than changing administrative borders?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by "changing the borders," I take it you mean in the sense I was referring to before, simply changing the course of the line on the map. And I can certainly agree that this article, at a minimum, relates to that, in that the other issue of the relationship with the federation or the rest of Yugoslavia would -- is in a different -- is more important than that, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this page be added to the same exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see again 65 ter 16278, page 3, to see how the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina governs the issue of exercising equality among peoples. Page 3 in both Serbian and English, Amendment 70, paragraph 10, the last paragraph of 10. I will read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters need a reference in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the interpreters need a reference to this matter in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 10: "A council shall ..." The last line of item 11 [as interpreted]. Item 10 is long, so it's the last part of 10: "The SRBH Assembly shall render ..." "The SRBH Assembly shall render decisions on matters concerning the fulfillment of the equality of the nations and nationalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the proposal of the council, through a special procedure established by the SRBH Assembly Rules of Procedure, with a two-thirds majority of the total number of deputies."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is stipulated by this article?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that even if two-thirds of the electorate turned out for the referendum and voted for independence, that decision also had to get a two-third majority in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, two-thirds of the total number of MPs, because a referendum is just a pre-condition to make that decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think it's clear the witness has said repeatedly that he doesn't purport to be a legal or constitutional scholar. I've been cautious about intervening because of trying to see if eventually this would come around to the real thrust of the witness's reports, but I think it becomes clear now the witness is being asked for constitutional/legal opinions, which he's repeatedly stated is not the focus of his expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, is it true that in your reports, you commented on my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: You're supposed to be responding to the observation of Mr. Tieger, not asking another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought to save time, because the witness will ultimately have to confirm this. I'm asking these questions in the light of his comments and the fact that his report deals with constitutional powers of various bodies in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party, later my position in Bosnia and Herzegovina as president of the Republika Srpska. These comments and his report refer to these matters all the time, and I can't avoid putting these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: There's a substantive difference between making an observation as to what's in the reports and asking Dr. Treanor to provide what is essentially a legal interpretation or opinion. It's the same as when you read out an article or part of an article to the witness and the best he can do is to say, Well, that's what it says. That's something that we can all see for ourselves. You might be much better placed, rather than seeking an interpretive comment upon something which is pretty obvious from the wording, itself, to moving on to anything in the nature of a challenge to the opinions that Dr. Treanor has set out in his reports.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would only like to ask

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that 83 deputies, who walked out of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and joined the Assembly of the Serbian People, make up more than one-third of 240 deputies in total?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this page be admitted, added to the same exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, it can be added.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although I'm not sure, in fact, whether there were only 230 [Realtime transcript read in error "240"] deputies in the Assembly, but, in any case, it's more than a third.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now that we have the constitutional and historical and legal framework of these events, I'll move to factual issues. And in the context of the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'll try to establish all the things that your reports deal with. We need to see whether the criterion of the broader context, which you named as your objective, is met. In 65 ter -- sorry, in document 12125, you said you tried to enumerate all the important events in their chronology?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I can go back to my previous answer, I said or I meant to say only 230 deputies in the Assembly. The transcript says "240."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, there were 240 deputies in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were 86 Serbs. Out of these 86, 84 were against secession, and 83 joined the Assembly of the Serbian People. On the premise that all the Serbs and Muslims and Croats and Yugoslavs and Jews, et cetera, were in favour of secession, do you agree, Dr. Treanor, that the remaining deputies in the Assembly could not, even then, vote for -- they could not have a majority over those 83?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, 83, irrespective of whether the total is 240 or 230, is more than a third. Therefore, the remaining deputies were less than two-thirds. I'm not sure what voting procedure we're talking about here. There doesn't seem to be any special majority required, from what we've seen of the Constitution, for passing a decision to hold a referendum, if that's what's being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we've just read that provision in the previous document, saying that a two-third majority is required in all matters regarding equality among peoples, and in all the constitutional matters everywhere in the world, a two-third majority is required. But let's go back to the chronology of events as presented in your reports. It is the position of the Defence that although you've invested great efforts to present the chronology of events, you left out the second boxer in the ring, by which I mean to say that events were not presented in a broader context. And to come back to the sports metaphor, one reads your report as if watching just one boxer in a match flailing his arms and not understanding why he's doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, if comments were permissible, then I'd say it's commented on before by Dr. Karadzic and redundant. But comments are not. The accused should move on to questions that are focused on the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic, you cannot really complain about the passing of time if you waste it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I was trying to use vivid language and to save time, but it seems I'm wasting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to say, Dr. Treanor, it is the position of the Defence that your reports do not provide a full picture, do not provide context, and the picture of events is distorted to our detriment. That's what I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's a comment. If you want to give a concrete example of what you say and put it to the witness, that's another thing, but a broad comment like that really doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is in the transcript, because I said, What do you say to that? Do you accept the position of the Defence? And if Dr. Treanor does not accept it, then we'll do what you suggest. If Dr. Treanor does not accept this proposition, we will provide many examples of what I just said; namely, that Dr. Treanor's reports do not provide context or a full picture of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I accept that your position is whatever you say it is. If I could go back to a question of context. I've been looking at this issue of the number of deputies in my report, and you mentioned the number of 83 deputies. As far as I can remember and as far as I can tell from my report, which does have a list of the deputies that were in the Assembly of the Serbian People, at this time there were only 78 of them. Later, in later years, there got to be 83 or 84. I think on this particular issue, it might be useful simply to look at the transcript of the session of the SRBH Assembly on the 25th or 26th of January, 1992, when they adopted the resolution on the referendum, to see what the vote was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I forgot to say that we have left that subject. Although not all deputies are present at all times, 83 expressed their wish to join the Assembly of the Serbian People. But we are now dealing with your report, and my objection -- my position was that you did not provide context, and now we are trying to establish this. Since we don't have much time, we won't be offering many documents, unless we have to because you disagree. Do you agree that changes to the Constitution of Croatia were made before the elections in 1990, in February, through Amendments 64 to 75 and 54 to 63? 54 to 63 and 64 to 75, those were the first changes to the Constitution, even before the elections, during socialist times?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd have to refresh my memory as to what those amendments were, but I'll accept your word for the fact that there were amendments at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know and do you agree that at the General Assembly of the Croatian Democratic Union, held in February 1990 in Zagreb, in the Lisinski hall, the president of that party, the future president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, said, among other things, the independent state of Croatia was not just a quisling creation and a fascist crime, but it was also an expression of the historic aspirations of the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this meeting, and I have seen the documents published in that connection. I can't recall this specific comment, but I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention to 25 July 1990, and in your report, 12125, paragraph 16, you state: "A mass rally of Serbs from all parts of Croatia ..." Please look at that paragraph. You say the Serb National Council was established by the Serbs at that time, and then at the end you say: "Serbian Assembly proclaimed to be invalid for the Serbs ..." [In English] "The Serbian Assembly proclaimed to be invalid for the Serbs all Croatian constitutional and legal changes which might negate their - that means Serb - sovereignty as a people and reduce their autonomous rights." [Interpretation] Is that right, that was the declaration of the independence and autonomy of the Serbian people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's what the paragraph says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 16, yes. Do you agree that on that same day, the 25th of July, 1990, the Parliament of Croatia adopted, for the second time in that year, amendments to the Constitution of Croatia and that the attribute "socialist" was eliminated from it, and the previous flag of Croatia was replaced by a chequer-board design?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I'm aware that there were amendments made to the Croatian Constitution. With the best will in the world, I can't remember the exact date or the purpose, although I thought that the flag of the Socialist Republic of Croatia also had a chequer-board design on it. But they may have changed the details of that design, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me remind you that Lord Owen, in his book, said -- on page 100 of the book, "The Balkan Odyssey," and I quote: "For the Serbs in Croatia, it was a provocation. Even if we take into account their historical ties, the fact that the government adopted the same symbol for its flag that Pavelic used, and that was the red-and-white chequer-board ..." Do we agree that Pavelic was the president of the quisling independent state of Croatia during the Second World War and that that state proclaimed racist laws based upon which different peoples, including Serbs, Jews and Roma, were killed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly generally correct, but I think what's in question here is the exact layout of the chequer-board on the flag. I think the Ustasha chequer-board is different than the Socialist chequer-board, and that certainly would have been regarded -- I can well say that the Serbs everywhere would have regarded that as being provocative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe that simultaneity of actions by the Serbs in Knin and by the parliament in Croatia should be emphasised, that the actions of the Serbs in Knin should not be regarded in isolation, but, rather, that they should be put in the context of the developments that were taking place in Zagreb at the same time? Do you agree that that would be necessary and, indeed, opportune?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there are many other facts than those adduced in this report which would certainly be useful to consider in connection with many of the issues raised. I tried to select the ones that I thought were most important and relevant to the report, with a view to keeping the length of the report within some reasonable bounds, but I certainly think that that is a useful fact or set of facts to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you confirmed for us that you knew that Croatia had been establishing its own secret army under various names; the Croatian National Guard, the Falcons Guards, the Volunteer Youth Units of the Civilian Protection of Croatia, and finally the National Corps Guard, the so-called ZNG, together with the MUP they constituted the nucleus of the Croatian military, and all that during the time when Croatia was still a republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll need a reference to the transcript. It's certainly my recollection is that while there was reference to arming made generally yesterday, this level of detail was not in any remote way adduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have a reference for that, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid that the misunderstanding stems from the transcript. I said that Dr. Treanor confirmed that both Izetbegovic and Tudjman were in the process of creating their own armies. He may have confirmed it even today. I wanted to ask Dr. Treanor whether he's familiar with these particular names, do these names ring any bells in addition to what already knows, all the names that I've given you. And the last name was the National Corps Guard, abbreviation being ZNG. They were established in May, and that together with the MUP or the police, those forces constituted the nucleus of the Croatian Army during the period when Croatia was still an integral part of Yugoslavia. If Dr. Treanor is familiar with these names and developments, then I don't need to call up any documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm generally familiar with those names and those general developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 17th of August, 1990, the Croatian Special Police carried out an attack on the police station in Benkovac. Benkovac is a Serbian municipality in Croatia. Do you know that they arrived, they attacked, they seized their weapons, that they disarmed the local Serbian police in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that particular action. I wouldn't be able to recall the exact date off the top of my head, and I couldn't confirm the details as you have set them out, but generally there was an action of that description around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on the 27th of September of that same year, the special units of the Croatian police stormed Petrinja in Banja, also a Serbian region, and that they arrested over 300 Serbs and that they confiscated weapons from the depots of the Territorial Defence and the Reserve Police?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same answer generally holds true for -- or does hold true for the -- for this question as for the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report, 12125, paragraph 18, you say that on the 30th September 1990, the results of the referendum were published and that they showed that of 567.317 votes, 567.127 or 99.97 per cent voted in favour of staying within Yugoslavia, and only 144 were against. Do you remember that paragraph? You're talking about the referendum of the Serbian people in Croatia, and that referendum dealt with Serbian autonomy.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the electoral body was almost 600.000 people and that on top of that we have to add 25 persons [as interpreted] under the age of 18, which means that there were far more than only 600.000 Serbs residing in Croatia at the time? Let's leave that. Maybe you don't know that. But the fact is that only persons who were of age could vote in that referendum, and not the 25 per cent of the people who were minors; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only people who were of age can vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on in your paragraphs 28 and 29 of the same document, you say that on the 21st of December, 1990, the Croatian leadership passed a resolution on the dissolution of Yugoslavia, and the Serbian leadership in Knin adopted a statute of the SAO Krajina. Paragraph 29 says: [In English] "The Croatian resolution foresaw the dissolution of the SFRY into several sovereign independent states within the existing republican boundaries."
